areas.group_intro: Mae Kessler, 6C. Antiques appraiser and the last of the Kessler Estate that owns the building (web I: 1893), bottle-green coat re-lined twice, silver pageboy, white cotton gloves worn as manners; certainty is not memory; contradiction is survivable (Bible IV.1, a case: antiques reporting incompatible provenance). Canon: white gloves by the door, a catalogue table, a packing station, gloved handling, a provenance cabinet composition (objects classified on walls, people kept close on furniture), two catalogue cards for one object in her hand (contradiction), the locked provenance drawer (hero object), nothing after 1935 which here means nothing after 1927, careful and spare, cleanliness 0.9, the second bedroom converted to a provenance archive, the monitor-top she has never replaced (one of the four). The 1912 Vantry prospectus is on her shelf and is the most disquieting object in the building (Bible VIII.3, VIII.5.h); she takes tea with Nadia on Thursdays and neither says the thing (web II.2). Proposed backstory: the Kessler Estate ledger sits beside the prospectus and is never opened. Build state: the main room has a sofa, coffee table, round table, old radio, oddments, catalogues, a sectional bookshelf and a radio; a second made bed in BED2; two wardrobes in the studio closet. The archive does not exist.

areas.title: Mae Kessler's kitchen
areas.location: Off the main room through the kitchen opening
areas.narrative: The kitchen is 1890 while the parlour is 1970 (Bible VIII.4): an enamel gas range on an angle-iron base, a sink with a drainboard, a wall cupboard, the sliding preparation cabinet, an electric monitor-top on splayed legs, new, expensive, noticeably loud, and the neighbours know who has one. What makes it Mae Kessler's is everything period-correct and nothing after 1935 (which here means nothing after 1927): a Hoosier-type cabinet in order, a covered butter dish, one good knife. One of the four electric flats: the monitor-top she has never replaced, kept pristine (enamel_pristine recipe); a covered butter dish; one good knife. Light is the kitchen linear or flush dome and the window; the Vantry point on the ceiling listens to the kettle.

areas.title: Mae Kessler's bathroom
areas.location: Private bathroom off the unit's private hall
areas.narrative: Every V2 bathroom is a windowless 1928 reopening room on one of the four roof ventilators: a painted gravity register, a cast-iron tub or shower receptor, a pedestal basin, a mirror medicine cabinet and a flush dome. What makes this one Mae Kessler's is a single adult who keeps things exact: one toothbrush, one glass, towel squared on the rail, nothing on the floor. Exact and old: a silver-backed brush set, a hair net, the pageboy's pins in a dish; the gloves never come in here. The room should pass the Shenmue test at the basin: evidence of construction (the register and its painted-over screws), attachment (the cabinet's two fixings), use (the wiping arc on the mirror), age (crazed enamel, a hairline in the tile), maintenance (a replacement chain on the plug) and consequence (a water line on the floor where the curtain leaks).

areas.group_intro: The roof. Eight storeys up (Bible III: B1, F01-F06, ROOF), reached by both stairs through bulkheads with doors that open and close normally. The 1928 reopening put four ILG-pattern electric ventilators here on four sheet-metal risers for the twenty-three windowless bathrooms (Bible VIII.5.i); the house tank stands on its timber legs southwest of the public bulkhead with the exposed ballcock the player services; the masonry chimney stands beside the east parapet; the guarded lift drive sits inside the public bulkhead. The prospectus drew the roof as a garden with people in it (Bible VIII.3); Malcolm keeps beds and communal planters and hands out rooted cuttings on Saturdays; Juno records up here Mon/Wed, Sacha photographs Tue/Thu, Iris sketches the light court at 13:00, Mae has her one unhurried hour on Sundays (schedules). The owner JSON lists the roof field, drainage and ventilator housings (A06) and the neighbouring tanks and aerials (A07) as pending; the membrane, coping, flashings, drainage, service weathering, chimney, tank, ventilators and lift drive each have their own Blender records. The smoke capture at 20:00 shows a dark deck under a star field with the tank, bulkheads, parapets and neighbouring masses; the player's lamp is the only light. What the roof lacks is use: no beds, no planters, no line, no watering can, no pigeon, no tar patch; the garden the prospectus promised is not here.

front_matter.subtitle: Every discrete area of the building, the street and the attached playable areas, reviewed from the current build and redesigned room by room
front_matter.lighting_state_short: production fixtures + player lamp, 20:00 frozen, teleported inspection
cover_paragraphs: This is a review-and-design document for the owner and for the implementing agents (ChatGPT/Codex). It walks every one of the 200 semantic spaces of the V2 blockout, the Vantry Arcade and its eleven shops, the Harukiya, the bodega, the service alley and the street, records what the current build shows at each station, and proposes numbered, placed, dimensioned changes with the canon they rest on and the acceptance view that would prove them.

It preserves working gameplay (every OPERATE, INSPECT and RESIST-REFUSE owner in the interaction matrix, the authored routes, door swings, care inspections and the Mina loop), it preserves intentional empty spaces (the sealed 2D and 3C, the fire-damaged 5D, the landlord's 6D, the funeral parlour's empty bier, the unfilled shelf in 3A), and it preserves architectural ownership: nothing here asks for a hand-edited glTF or JSON, and every placement is relative to an existing anchor, fixture or wall.

Proposed backstory is labelled as such everywhere it appears and is never promoted to canon by this document. Where the build and the Bible disagree, the disagreement is recorded in the canon findings and the Bible is treated as prevailing until amended.

sections.title: How to use this dossier
blocks: Each area page carries five parts: identity (exact space id, location, users, authored size), current evidence (captioned views from the current build with the station recorded, observed problems separated from interpretations), a room narrative (what happened here and what the player should infer), numbered changes with stable ids of the form SPACE_ID-nnn, and implementation notes (sources, dependencies, what must be preserved, and the view or action that demonstrates success). Unknown measurements are marked unknown or given as ranges rather than invented.

The change register (change_register.csv / .xlsx / .json) is the editable copy of every numbered change with one row per change and empty status and owner_notes columns. The coverage checklist (coverage_checklist.csv) lists every area with its coverage class. dossier.json is the complete machine-readable document; images/ holds the review tiles; evidence/ holds the sweep records, receipts and the full-resolution capture inventory.

bullets: Priority P1: the room reads wrong from the doorway or the resident is not legible. P2: strengthens the story, period truth or the Shenmue test. P3: polish.
Action: add / move / refine / remove / keep. Keep rows exist to protect intentional emptiness.

Signal: every change states whether the object carries a signal. If it does, Bible VIII.2 licenses it forty years early (Bakelite, brass, cloth flex, repairable). If it does not, it is 1927 and second-hand.
Family rooms (bathrooms, vestibules, private halls, kitchens, halls, cores, service halls, roof decks) share a standard set and add a per-resident delta; the delta is where the identity lives.

Building-wide findings (post-1950 furniture variants, tile on both wall faces, floating ducts, the bare service spine, bare windows, bedding and curtains, sourceless cool light, missing radios, the fridge count) are numbered once as BW-001 to BW-014 on the building-wide page and cited from the room pages; fix the family, not the room.

sections.title: Queens, November 1928: the period notes the rooms rest on
blocks: The Orison is a 1912 Vantry demonstration block, partially demolished in 1927 and reopened in 1928 as flats (Bible VIII.5.h). Everything a resident owns they owned in 1927; the building's paper trail begins in 1928. The following are ordinary facts of a Queens apartment house of that year, used here as texture, not as new canon.

bullets: Services: one-pipe steam from a hand-fired coal boiler, coal delivered through a street cover to a chute; gas ranges; iceboxes with ice cards in the window and an iceman's rounds; a dumbwaiter for ash and groceries; a brass Cutler mail chute or bank; push-button double light switches; pull chains on closet lights; a Vantry point on every ceiling in place of anything that could be mistaken for a detector.

Finishes: plaster on brick, wallpaper in the front rooms, painted wainscot in halls, oak strip floors in rooms, linoleum in kitchens, hexagonal white tile and subway tile in bathrooms, terrazzo in the lobby, enamel paint over everything that was once varnished.

Objects: Bakelite only for moulded things; cloth-braided flex in good flats and stiff rubber flex in poor ones (wealth reads through wiring); tin, enamel, cast iron, copper, brass and no aluminium or stainless; rayon new and everywhere; no zips; valves sold in printed sleeves at the bodega.

Street: horse drays beside motor cars and a rail-less tram (the authored wrong five percent); milk and ice by cart; newsstands; a locksmith, a hand laundry venting steam, a druggist's show globes; a storm at both ends of the street and a railway proposed to cross them.
Season: the Saturday after the Hoover-Smith election, wet and cold, coal smoke, the first frost; windows scraped from the inside in the morning (Bible VIII.2).

Signal: anything that carries, captures, switches, stores or reproduces a signal is forty years early. The listening head, the brass signal outlet by every socket, the dial-less house telephone with the player as operator, the witness clocks, the receiving cabinets and the radios are better made than anything else in the building and are also twenty years old and repaired by four people.

sections.title: Proposed backstory register (additions, not canon)
blocks: Every backstory addition in this dossier is listed on the room page where it is used, marked PROPOSED BACKSTORY, and collected here so the owner can accept or strike them in one place. None contradicts a ruling; several extend the relationship web's tentative threads into objects.

bullets: 1A Evelyn Marsh: the class register of 1954 is on her study shelf with one name underlined twice (web II.6, the Red Pencil); the spare guest cup was bought for a visit that did not happen in 1927.
1D Teresa Vale: the office became the night station the week she moved in; the call bell she cannot unplug is a Vantry house bell wired before the building had tenants.
2A Mina Vale: the unlabelled box holds the stenotype paper of one afternoon in court; the caption wall is arranged so the four-second gap has one blank card.
2B Lena Ortiz: the repair queue has three garments from this building (Cam's jersey, Teresa's cape lining, Peter's collar) tagged with floor numbers instead of names.
2C Juno Kells: the recording room's blanket wall is pinned with the rail of a stolen session archive; one reel box is labelled only with a date in 1927 (take 18, web II.7).
3A Malcolm Reed: the propagation bench grows cuttings for the whole building; the empty memorial pot sits above the sink where the light is best and the plant would have been happiest.
3B Omar Bell: the sacrificial teardown is a radio chassis from the night of the 1977 blackout (web I), kept broken on purpose; his notes to the super are notes to himself.
3D Rhea Sato: the error archive is a card index; the dressing mirror faces away from the booth so that she never watches herself make a mistake.
4A Peter Wren: a folded composition-paper note reading only See me, in red, lives in the wallet (web II.6); the unresolved form at each station is the same form, 11-B, at different stages.
4B the player: the previous tenant left one thing in the closet, a service cap with the wrong initials inside the band (web II.9, Mara Chen).
4C Cam and Noel: the negotiated table has a chalk line under the oilcloth; Noel's museum shelf holds three objects from the family flat before the trial (web II.1).
4D Transient Guests: the locked owner closet holds the lost property of nine previous guests, each item tagged with a date and a room number that is always 4D.
5A Nadia Quell: the corrected floor plan of this building on the icebox door shows a room that is not on the blockout; the rent-strike ledger is signed Management.
5B Cal Dwyer: the Delayed Voice Reel is on the shelf in a plain box among the dated tapes, unmarked but for a courthouse date (web II.1); never audible.
5C Iris Bell: the failed canvases facing the wall are portraits of one man she stopped letting look (web II.3).
6A Sacha Reed: the contact sheet of the motif is pinned above the charging bench; one print of Malcolm's plant is the only picture of a plant in the flat (web II.8).
6B Jonah Price: the rejected endings in the wastebasket are all the same chapter; the bed faces the desk.
6C Mae Kessler: the 1912 Vantry prospectus is on the shelf beside the Kessler Estate ledger that is never opened (web II.2); two catalogue cards for one object lie on the table.
The Harukiya: the grand fabric came from a closed hotel bar in 1927; the two photographs show the block in 1913 and 1919 (ledger A0.5).
The shops: the Model Laundry and the Photo Supplies hold things for people who did not come back; Keys Cut keeps a register of every key cut in the Orison; the Radio Service set is tuned to 1610.

blocks: art/data/v2_owner_improvement_20261008.json records 40 owner-reviewed items: lobby instruments, registers and tour key, house telephone board, dumbwaiter, fuse panel, tank mechanism, alley and shed work lights (G01-G07), Harukiya loudspeakers, piano and microphone, phonautograph, darts, receiving cabinets, signage and task-lamp cords (G08-G14, all implemented and reviewed), the finish families T01-T16 (implemented and reviewed, T07/T09 pending final review), T17 plants in progress, A01-A04 apartment light/plaster/floor, public floors and joinery, bedding and basement context (implemented, A01/A02 pending final review), and A05-A08 (exterior stone trim, roof field and drainage, neighbouring tanks and aerials, lift cab paneling) still pending. This dossier does not re-propose those families; where a room depends on one, the dependency is named.

The fabrication coverage index (art/blender/v2_fabrication_coverage.md) and the 2026-10-05 space sweep (art/blender/v2_space_review.json) are the previous whole-building reviews; this dossier supersedes neither as evidence and adds the room-by-room design layer on top of them.

sections.title: The layout workbench and the legacy plan
blocks: tools/room_layout_workbench.py draws plans from art/data/building_layout.json, which is the legacy (V1) source context: its room ids (F02_A_MAIN, F01_COMMON_B, F01_STORAGE_C) and furniture footprints describe the building the V2 rebuild replaced. The V2 authority is game/data/orison_v2_blockout.json with 200 semantic spaces, 1,104 anchors, 111 doors, 87 openings and 72 windows. Where a V2 space keeps a legacy id (the main rooms, beds and baths of 2A, 2B, 3A, 3B, 4A, 4B, 5A, 5B, 5C, 6A, 6B, 6C) the workbench packet is a useful second opinion on furniture footprints; where V2 renamed or split a room (vestibules, private halls, studies, studios, the lobby suite, the service halls) the workbench has no record and the plans in this dossier were drawn from the blockout instead. Reconciliation rule: the blockout rect and anchors win; the legacy packet informs only the furniture dimensions it still shares.
